https://www.hurriyetdailynews.com/otokar.text: Otokar begins Romanian-built COBRA II deliveries News Economy July 27 2026 09:55:04 Otokar begins Romanian-built COBRA II deliveries Deliveries of COBRA II 4x4 tactical wheeled armored vehicles produced entirely in Romania have begun for the Romanian Armed Forces, marking a new phase in Türkiye’s largest-ever single armored land vehicle export project. The program covers 1,059 COBRA II vehicles ordered by Romania. Following the delivery of vehicles manufactured in Türkiye, the first COBRA II units produced at the Automecanica Mediaș facility in Romania have now been handed over to the Romanian military. With serial production progressing as planned, Otokar ’s Mediaș facility has become the company’s manufacturing hub in Europe and its first production site within the European Union. The development gives Romania the capability to carry out all stages of production for a 4x4 armored vehicle rather than simply assembling imported components. More than 780 of the 1,059 vehicles ordered by Romania are scheduled to be produced in Mediaș over a five-year period. Around 300 vehicles have been delivered so far, while 216 units, including four new variants, are planned for delivery during 2026. Yusuf Fettahlıoğlu, General Manager of Automecanica Mediaș, said the Mediaș facility is expected to evolve into a regional land-systems hub capable of supporting future export opportunities within NATO and European Union defense programs, in addition to meeting the needs of the Romanian Armed Forces. The 140,000-square-meter facility has been equipped to NATO standards and operates according to the same production standards used at Otokar’s facilities in Türkiye. Since its introduction in 2013, the COBRA II has been selected by more than 20 users in 13 countries, including over 600 vehicles operated by NATO members. The vehicle is currently in service in 30 different variants worldwide. Photograph: Hiro Komae/AP US military US marine arrested in Japan on suspicion of killing woman, police say Suspect allegedly killed woman at hotel in Okinawa as prime minister calls crime ‘exceptionally brutal and vicious’ Agence France-Presse and Guardian staff Sun 4 Oct 2026 09.46 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A US marine stationed on Japan ’s southern island of Okinawa is accused of murdering a Japanese woman and has been arrested on suspicion of murder, police said on Sunday. The suspect allegedly “killed [a] 39-year-old woman at a hotel in Naha and stole her wallet” as well as her backpack, local police told news media outlets. Citing police, NBC News reported that the suspect charged in the case was identified Lance Cpl Devin Jacob Ballard, 20. Anna Yagi was identified as the victim. Ballard denied the allegations, police said, according to NBC. Crimes including rapes, assaults, hit-and-run and drunk-driving accidents by US personnel have long sparked protests on Okinawa. The island bears a disproportionate burden of hosting about 70% of US military facilities in Japan. US ambassador George Glass posted on social media that he had spoken with Japan’s foreign ministry and Okinawa’s governor, offering “sincere condolences to the victim’s family” and pledging cooperation into the investigation of her death. The Japanese prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, said Japan had lodged a protest with US authorities and called the crime “exceptionally brutal and vicious”. The government has urged the US “to provide maximum cooperation with the investigation, enforce stricter discipline among US military personnel, and take thorough measures to prevent the recurrence of similar crimes,” Takaichi said. Public broadcaster NHK and other Japanese media outlets, citing investigation sources, reported that CCTV footage from near the scene showed a foreign man entering a room with a woman and later leaving with her belongings. Police then found a 20-year-old man who matched the description of the suspect seen in the footage and asked him to accompany them voluntarily to a local police station where he was arrested, NHK reported. “We have lost a family member and are deeply saddened,” Yagi’s brother said through local police, according to the Asahi Shimbun daily newspaper. “My parents, in particular, are utterly devastated at the loss of their daughter.” The US has about 54,000 military personnel stationed in Japan, mostly on Okinawa. Crimes committed by US personnel in Japan have been a thorn in relations between the close security allies. “Incidents and accidents involving US military personnel cause great anxiety among the local community and must not be allowed to happen,” Japan’s defense minister Shinjiro Koizumi said. In June 2025, a Japanese court sentenced US marine Jamel Clayton – then 22 – to seven years in prison after being convicted of choking and sexually assaulting a woman in her 20s. Earlier, in 2017, former US marine and civilian military base worker Kenneth Shinzato was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa. The same year, US forces in Japan banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after an intoxicated American marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing its 61-year-old local driver. According to the Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper, about 6,000 US military personnel have been arrested since Okinawa was returned to Japan from the US in 1972 after the second world war. The number of arrests in a year hit 80 in 2024, the highest in 20 years. https://www.thepoultrysite.com/articles/.text: Health & disease Diseases Virulent Newcastle disease Newcastle Disease in Europe: the one-serotype protection strategy against Genotype VII What producers need to know about vaccine protection, vaccination execution and transmission control. 29 September 2026 11 minute read By: Jessica Lee DVM Europe Key Takeaways Newcastle Disease (ND) is re-emerging across Europe, with confirmed outbreaks since 2024 in Poland, the Czech Republic, Germany, Spain and, as of September 2026, Hungary. All NDV field strains belong to a single serotype (APMV-1), so therefore standard vaccines (e.g. LaSota, B1) still can neutralize Genotype VII NDV: a change in genotype does not mean a change in serotype or a loss of vaccine-induced protection. Most outbreaks in vaccinated flocks trace back to failures in vaccination (delivery) or immunisation (host response), not to a vaccine or genotype mismatch. Because ND vaccines rarely provide sterile immunity, controlling transmission (not just clinical protection) is essential to stopping spread between houses and farms. HVT-vectored vaccines, such as Vectormune® ND, bypass maternal antibody interference and has been shown to cut the reproductive number (R) for Genotype VII NDV from 3.20 (unvaccinated) to 0.82 (vaccinated). Not all HVT-vectored vaccines perform equally: insertion site, promoter, donor strain and HVT passage level all affect real-world protection. After decades of relative silence, Newcastle Disease (ND) has returned to the forefront of European poultry industry with alarming speed. Early 2026, ND cases were reported in western European countries which used to be calm like Germany which had not seen ND for the last 30 years. And in early September, Hungary officially confirmed the presence of ND in Fülöpháza, Bács-Kiskun County (Kecskemét district) affecting up to 240,000 birds, marking its first occurrence of the disease in Hungarian commercial poultry in more than three decades, with the last official report dating back to 1992. Updated from: EU Animal Diseases Information System (ADIS) until 16th September 2026 While historically viewed by many European producers as an exotic threat, recent epidemiological developments with Genotype VII, demonstrate that ND virus (NDV) is still actively expanding across the continent. Since 2024, field cases have surged in Poland and the Czech Republic following initial transboundary movements near the Belarusian border. Until June 2026, eastern and southern Germany reported over 60 confirmed outbreaks, spanning dense poultry regions around Berlin and Bavaria, plus Saxony-Anhalt. Concurrently, beyond Central Europe, Spain has emerged as one of the most severely affected countries with the virus returned in December 2025 after disease-free status since 2022, spreading in distinct waves in Valencia initially then in areas like Valladolid in June, later to adjacent areas like Segovia, Salamanca, and Ávila in July and August; these outbreaks in Spain have been affecting up to 2.2 million birds in both small and large commercial broilers and layers farms. This sudden emergence poses an immediate commercial and regulatory risk. Because virulent ND is a mandatory notifiable disease governed by strict statutory controls—EU legislation requires mandatory flock depopulation, movement standstills, tracing zones, and severe export restrictions—the financial burden of an outbreak frequently comparable to High Pathogenicity Avian Influenza (HPAI). Image (AI): Newcastle Disease infected broilers showing torticollis in the farm Does a new genotype mean vaccines no longer work? According to World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) CHAPTER 3.3.14. Newcastle Disease is caused by virulent strains of Avian Paramyxovirus type 1 (APMV-1) of the genus Orthoavulavirus (AOAV) belonging to the family Paramyxoviridae. At present, the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses (ICTV) had defined up to 22 serotypes of avian paramyxoviruses designated APMV-1 to APMV-22 affecting a broad range of wild and domestic avian species. Each distinct APMV serotype represents a fundamentally different virus to the host immune system. However, within poultry production, APMV-1 (AOAV-1) is the ONLY agent responsible for classic ND. What does this mean? It means all NDV strains share a single immunological appearance (“look”), the fundamental surface proteins responsible for inducing neutralizing antibodies. This allows for universal cross-protection where a properly primed immune system by any standard AOAV-1 (eg. B1 or La Sota) vaccine is able to recognize and neutralize virulent field challenge strains regardless of whether they are classified as Genotype II, Genotype V, Genotype VII, Genotype XIII, or Genotype XXI. In contrast, genotyping is based on the internal genetic code, defined by the actual nucleotide sequence (of the Fusion [ ] protein gene specifically). As NDV is an RNA viruses, it is not surprising that point mutations naturally occur over time when it replicates, creating different "genotypes", hence identifying dozens of NDV strains which belongs to different phylogenetic branches. Up until today, according to Dimitrov et al. 2019, there are 21 genotypes (I – XXI) have been identified and classified based on the complete F gene (1,662 nucleotides) sequence. In short, genotyping is essentially relevant for epidemiology and surveillance purposes but change in genotype does not means a change in serotypes or loss of vaccine-induced protection. The genotype currently circulating in Europe and dominating global panzootics—Genotype VII—is genetically distinct from historical legacy strains such as LaSota (Genotype II) or Herts 33/56 (Genotype IV). Once again, as Genotype VII also belongs to serotype APMV-1 (AOAV-1), the neutralizing antibodies generated from another standard AOAV-1 (eg. B1 or La Sota), will be able to recognize Genotype VII and neutralize it. With this, producers do not need to constantly update or custom-manufacture vaccines every time a new genotype or sub-genotype is identified in the field. Existing, high-quality commercial vaccines on the market are biologically capable of providing robust protection against today's circulating European field strains. Why outbreaks still sometimes happen in vaccinated flocks? Since all Newcastle Disease viruses belong to one serotype and commercial vaccines cross-protect against Genotype VII, why do field breakdowns and clinical outbreaks still occur in vaccinated flocks? To answer this, producers must evaluate their operational processes through three distinct definitions: 1. Vaccine - the product A high-quality, stable biological preparation containing the target protective antigen. Conventional live and inactivated ND vaccines have served the industry for decades, but they carry inherent operational limitations. Live and inactivated, whether is from attenuated whole ND virus such as LaSota or B1 strain or recently available reverse genetic genotype-matching vaccines, are sensitive to ND maternally derived antibody (ND-MDA) interference which subsequently reduced their efficacy in commercial birds (usually provided with high ND-MDA) when compared to the results in laboratory using Specific Pathogens Free (SPF) birds with no ND-MDA. Furthermore, conventional live and inactivated vaccines mainly only provide mucosal and humoral immunity, respectively, which is not enough to further reduce virus shedding in field situation. New technology using Herpesvirus of Turkeys (HVT) as a viral vector expressing the key protective Fusion (F) protein gene of NDV can bypasses MDA and not been neutralized by circulating NDV MDA, allowing reliable and effective early-life administration in the hatchery. Besides, being HVT-vectored, this vaccine provides strong cellular and humoral immunity plus mucosal immunity that can further reduce virus shedding. Lastly, as a herpesvirus, this vector elicits life-long continuous immune stimulations which greatly simplies the vaccination protocols. 2. Vaccination - the administration process Vaccination refers strictly to the physical delivery of the vaccine product to the bird. A failure at this stage simply means the vaccine will never have a chance to work properly. Common field failures during vaccination include: Cold-chain break : Exposure of live or vector vaccines to temperature spikes during transport or storage. Water quality issues : Presence of chlorine, heavy metals, or sanitizers in drinking water systems during mass live administration can neutralizes live vaccine viruses. Image (AI): Drinker line with biofilm that consists of a complex matrix of bacteria, algae, organic matter, and extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) lining the inside of water pipes. This organic load physically traps and inactivates delicate live vaccine viruses before they can reach the birds. Poor application and delivery technique : Inadequate waterline priming, incorrect water deprivation timing or uneven drinker line access can lead to inconsistent vaccine uptake in the house. Uneven spray droplet size, poorly calibrated sprayers, or incorrect in-ovo/ subcutaneous injection techniques can leave a percentage of the flock completely unvaccinated or receiving suboptimal doses of vaccines. This will leave a critical percentage of flocks vulnerable to field challenge. Image (AI): When birds are left unconfined during spray vaccination, they will naturally run away from the applicator which creates coverage gaps, leaving a significant portion of the flock under-vaccinated. Image (AI): When birds rush for water, the dominant and large birds will get access first and block other smaller birds. Such chaos usually will end up with poor and uneven vaccine coverage in the flock. 3. Immunization - the biological outcome Immunization is the successful physiological development of protective immunity within the bird following vaccination. Even with proper vaccine delivery, true immunization can fail due to host or environmental factors: High levels of circulating ND-MDA can neutralize conventional live and inactivated ND vaccines administered in early life, preventing proper immune response. Co-infections with early infection on reassorted Infectious Bursal Disease virus (IBDv) or exposure to feed mycotoxins impair the bird’s immune system, preventing it from mounting a robust response. Sub-optimal brooding temperatures, high ammonia levels, high stocking density, and nutritional deficiencies impair immune performance. Outdated vaccination program (timing, type of vaccines used and route of vaccination) may not build peak immunity fast enough to protect birds to face early strong challenge. When an outbreak occurs in a vaccinated region, the actual culprit is rarely a “vaccine escape strain” or a genotype mismatch. In almost all cases, investigation reveals a breakdown in vaccination execution or host immunization inhibitors. How can vaccination reduce Newcastle Disease transmission, and not only clinical signs? At this point, undeniably that vaccination remains one of the most important tools to control and prevent Newcastle Disease together with biosecurity and control of movement. But how much do we expect from vaccination against ND? Vaccination can protect birds against mortality and severe clinical signs. However, clinical protection is only half of the success when facing ND challenge. Since vaccines usually do not provide sterile immunity, vaccinated birds can still be infected without showing major clinical signs, and at the same time shedding the field virus into the environment especially Genotype VII-known for particularly high viral shedding. This is when control of transmission by a vaccine becomes very critical in managing this virus. The goal is to not only save infected birds, but also to limit total cases, reduce viral shedding, and shorten shedding duration. Cutting these three variables will lowers environmental contamination and breaks the chain of infection within the house, between houses, and eventually from farm to farm. In 2020, Tatár-Kis et. al, published the evidence demonstrated for the first time that administration of HVT-vectored ND vaccine, Vectormune® ND, at day-old significantly blocked horizontal bird-to-bird transmission of velogenic Genotype VII ND in addition to significant reduced viral shedding and 100% clinical protection in both directly challenged and co-mingled contact vaccinated broilers. This clinical efficacy was accompanied by a R (Reproductive number) value of 0.82 (less than 1) only in vaccinated birds compared to 3.20 in unvaccinated birds. This isn't just theory — if we translate this to modern poultry production complexes, having R-value below 1 means vaccinated birds will shed significantly less virus into the litter and air in case of infection. Eventually it will lower the environmental contamination and keeping the virus from spreading to next house or neighbouring farms. The bottom line, instead of having an uncontrollable wildfire that spreads through the whole complex, Genotype VII virus challenge becomes a small campfire that runs out of fuel and fades out. This is a real gamechanger to win the battle, since true transmission control is finally possible. What makes an HVT-Vectored Newcastle Disease vaccine different from one another? HVT-vectored vaccines vary fundamentally in their construct based on four key genetic variables: the insertion site of the NDV Fusion (F) gene (may affect virus replication) the promoter (important to drive antigen expression) the sources strain of the donor F gene (may determines immunogenicity) the passage level of the HVT viral backbone (lower passage level of HVT in cell culture gives earlier viremia in birds) Vectormune® ND stands apart from other HVT-vectored ND vaccines with patented insertion site at UL 45/46 and PEC promoter, therefore this vaccine drives optimal, robust expression of the NDV Fusion ( ) protein. This proprietary design ensures stable viral replication without compromising host cell dynamics, directly translating into superior immunological performance. Controlled studies in commercial birds demonstrate that this unique rHVT-ND construct enables a significantly faster onset of immunity compared to other recombinant vector vaccines. When challenged with virulent Genotype VII field strains, Vectormune® ND induced faster protection, establishing earlier onset of immunity and stronger reduction of viral shedding compared to its competitor. Furthermore, the vaccine's broad-spectrum efficacy is supported by extensive scientific validation. Over 75 challenge studies have confirmed strong, reliable protection against a wide array of geographically diverse genotypes and sub-genotypes—most notably very virulent Genotype VII.1.1 and Genotype VII.2 strains. This extensive body of evidence highlights how its distinctive construction delivers consistent, long-term cross-protection across today's global ND threats. Take home message In conclusion, the re-emergence of Newcastle Disease across Europe is a clear signal that ND is a growing risk requiring heightened vigilance. Outbreaks in Poland, Germany, Spain and Hungary does not mean the current available vaccines are ineffective. By shifting focus from theoretical genotype-matching to understanding the difference between vaccines type, quality of vaccination and flock immunization, we could identify the real reason of the breaks. Producers do not need not to panic about genetic drift or emerging genotype labels as biological facts are reassuring that all ND viruses remain ONE single serotype. By deploying advanced vector solutions like Vectormune® ND that has proven result in control transmission against Genotype VII alongside field live ND vaccination and rigorous biosecurity, the European poultry industry possesses all the tools required to control ND and maintain long-term flock health and profitability.
